PMC3557905-s0-p0.reader: This is the whole paper compressed into one paragraph, written last and read first. Cas9 is a bacterial protein that cuts DNA wherever a short guide RNA points it. The claims here are that the two assemble inside human cells, that cutting needs both of them, that something about the guide RNA is the bottleneck, and that lengthening the guide helped. Everything after this paragraph is the evidence for those four claims. Read them as claims for now, and decide at the end which ones the experiments actually carried.
PMC3557905-s0-p0.caution: “In human cells” is doing a lot of work here. Hold onto that phrase — you’ll be asked what it actually covers.

PMC3557905-s1-p0.reader: Cutting both strands of DNA at a chosen spot, a double-strand break, is how you edit a genome: the cell repairs the cut and you steer the repair. Two earlier tools did it, zinc-finger nucleases and TALENs, a nuclease being a protein that cuts DNA. Both needed a new protein built for every target, and both sometimes cut the wrong place.

PMC3557905-s1-p1.reader: Bacteria defend themselves against viruses with a system called CRISPR, which stores scraps of invader DNA and destroys that DNA if it returns. One version needs a single protein, Cas9, to do the cutting. A short piece of RNA, a single-stranded relative of DNA, tells Cas9 where: a 20-letter guide sequence matching the target. Researchers had already simplified that guide into one piece, the sgRNA. That is what makes it useful. One protein plus one short RNA cuts DNA wherever you choose, provided the target sits beside a short landing signal called a PAM. Change the RNA, change the target. Whether any of it worked in human cells was still unknown.

PMC3557905-s1-p2.reader: This is the authors saying what they will show. Cas9 can be made inside a human cell, reach the nucleus where the DNA sits, and pair with its guide RNA. Together they cut, and the cell patches the break by glueing the ends back together, often losing or adding a few letters. Nothing happens unless both parts are present. Treat it as a promise: the experiments that follow decide whether it holds.

PMC3557905-s2-p0.reader: First they had to show the parts work at all. They picked a human gene to aim at, one an older cutting tool had already been built for, which gives them something to compare against. They put Cas9 into human cells grown in a dish, tagged with a glowing green marker so they could see where it went, and with a short address label attached that tells the cell to carry it into the nucleus. Figure 1B shows it arriving there, and Figure 1A shows the protein is whole rather than chopped up. They then supplied the guide RNA: a stretch of letters matching the target, plus a folded tail that Cas9 grips. Figure 1D shows the guide is made, and that more of it survives when Cas9 is present, which hints the two hold on to each other.
PMC3557905-s2-p0.caution: Notice how many genes and how many cell types are in play. The abstract’s phrasing suggested something broader.

PMC3557905-s2-p1.reader: Now the real question: does anything actually get cut? You cannot watch a cut happen, so they looked for its scar. A cell repairing a double-strand break by glueing the ends together often loses or gains a few letters. They copied the target region out of many cells, mixed the copies so strands from different cells could pair, and added an enzyme that cuts only where two strands disagree. A signal means some copies differ from others, which the authors read as a cut clumsily repaired. Follow that chain rather than the conclusion. Figure 1E shows the signal. A tool already known to cut this region ran alongside it.

PMC3557905-s2-p2.reader: Editing worked, but weakly, so they asked which ingredient was running short. They broke the cells open and gave the resulting soup a piece of target DNA to cut, which lets them test the machinery outside a living cell where the amounts can be controlled. Soup from cells given only Cas9 did nothing to the target. Add guide RNA made separately in a tube, and the same soup cut it well (Figure 2A). Soup from cells given both Cas9 and the guide did cut. And when extra guide RNA was added on top of that, activity rose again (Figure 2B). Four conditions, four outcomes. The differences between them are the finding.

PMC3557905-s2-p3.reader: They next tried making the guide hold on to Cas9 better. Two longer versions were built, adding extra paired letters to the stretch Cas9 grips, plus a few more at the very end, copying the shape the bacterium uses naturally (Figure 3A). Both were put back into cells with Cas9 and tested the same way as before. The longer guides appear to cut more (Figure 3B). Take that as a lead rather than a settled result. The last sentence of this paragraph is where the authors say how much weight it will bear, and it is worth reading more slowly than the rest.

PMC3557905-s3-p0.reader: Here they step back and weigh what they have. They open by naming where this could go: human therapies, agriculture, engineering microbes. All of it works the same way, by making a cut at a chosen place and letting the cell's own repair machinery do the rest, which is why a reliable way to aim the cut matters so much. Their contribution, they say, is that the aiming is done by a guide RNA rather than by a purpose-built protein. They report an efficiency figure for editing at their target, and set it against the older tool. They state where they think the limit on performance lies, and list ideas for lifting it: better guide design, more of it, protective additions to the guide's ends. Those are proposals, not results. The claim worth watching is the last one. They argue their system is the better one because changing target means rewriting a short RNA instead of engineering a new protein. That is a fair point about convenience, and they place it directly beside the efficiency comparison. Easier to aim is not the same as better at cutting.
PMC3557905-s3-p0.caution: The paper says “suggest”, not “show”. That word is a deliberate choice by the authors — watch for it.

PMC3557905-s3-p1.reader: They close by looking ahead. One cell could be given several guide RNAs at once, they suggest, either to hit a single gene harder or to go after several genes together. That would matter for work across whole genomes, or for building models of diseases that involve more than one gene. Read this paragraph for what it is: a proposal about what the tool might allow, arriving at the end of a paper about what it did.

PMC3557905-s4-p0.reader: Building the tools. The bacterial Cas9 gene was rewritten letter by letter so human cells would read it efficiently, since the same protein can be spelled many ways and bacteria and humans favour different spellings. Three things were bolted on: a tag for detecting the protein, an address label sending it to the nucleus, and a glowing marker for seeing it. Each was ordered as synthetic DNA and slotted into rings of DNA that human cells will read from.

PMC3557905-s4-p1.reader: Growing and treating the cells. They used a human cell line grown in a dish, the kind that grows reliably and takes up foreign DNA easily, which is why a line like this is the usual choice for a first test. The cells were fed a nutrient broth and kept at body temperature. The DNA rings carrying Cas9 and the guide were then delivered using a reagent that ferries DNA across the cell membrane. They deliberately supplied more of the guide RNA plasmid than of the Cas9 plasmid. They also checked what fraction of cells took the DNA up at all, using the glowing marker to count them. Two days later the cells were burst open and the contents divided up for the tests that follow.

PMC3557905-s4-p2.reader: Checking Cas9 is really there and whole. Proteins from burst cells were sorted by size on a gel, then stained with something that sticks to the tag they added. The right-sized band means success.

PMC3557905-s4-p3.reader: How the edits were counted. They copied the target region out of the cells' DNA, heated the copies until the two strands came apart, then let them cool so strands re-paired at random. An edited strand paired with an unedited one leaves a bulge where the letters disagree, and the enzyme they add cuts only at bulges. Running the result through a gel separates the cut pieces from the uncut ones, and comparing how much lands in each gives an estimate of how much editing happened. Separately, they read individual copies letter by letter, by first growing each one on its own in bacteria so that every copy read came from a single original molecule. That is how they could say which letters had been lost or gained at the cut site.
PMC3557905-s4-p3.caution: Ask yourself what this assay can and can’t tell you. It measures something, but possibly not the thing you assume.

PMC3557905-s4-p4.reader: Making guide RNA in a tube, not in cells. Two DNA strands formed a template, an enzyme copied it into RNA, and a gel cleaned it up. This is the spare guide.

PMC3557905-s4-p5.reader: Checking the guide RNA is present, and how much. Small RNAs were pulled out of the cells, sorted by size on a gel, and moved onto a membrane where they were fixed in place. A short radioactive DNA probe, built to stick only to the guide sequence, was washed over it. Wherever the probe stuck, the film darkens. This is the test behind the earlier claim that the guide survives better when Cas9 is around.

PMC3557905-s4-p6.reader: The cut-in-a-tube test. Contents of burst cells were mixed with a ring of DNA carrying the target, held at body temperature for an hour, then cut with a second enzyme at a known spot. That second cut is the trick: it turns a successful Cas9 cut into two fragments of predictable size, so those two sizes on a gel are what the authors take as evidence that Cas9 cut where it was supposed to, rather than somewhere random.
